name: Global Privacy Control
plain: Browser signal that the person opts out of sale or sharing of data.
meaning: Legally binding opt-out in California, Colorado, Connecticut and more, so sites must honor it. Also tells the site this user runs privacy-focused settings or a browser like Firefox, DuckDuckGo or Brave.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

chrome.note: Not shipped; extensions add the header

firefox.note: Opt-in setting; default in Private Browsing optional

limits.headline: Can see that you asked sites not to sell or share your data
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it with each page request if the setting is on
can: Check the Global Privacy Control signal
Treat it as your opt out of sale or sharing, where the law requires it, such as in California
Learn that you may use a privacy focused browser or setting
cannot: Make a site honor it outside places where the law requires it
See your name or account from this signal
Work by default in Chrome or Safari; you need an extension or a privacy browser
limits.differs: Firefox, Brave and DuckDuckGo send it. Chrome and Safari do not by default.

story.what_it_is: A browser signal that tells sites not to sell or share your data.

marketing.name: Global Privacy Control
marketing.pitch: The group describes a simple browser setting that sends an opt out request about selling or sharing data to every site.

marketing.name: Global Privacy Control
marketing.pitch: Mozilla explains a Firefox setting that tells sites you do not want your data sold or shared.

story.for_you: If you turn it on, every site gets a note saying 'do not sell or share my data'. You may see fewer targeted ads, or a banner saying your choice was honored. In some places the law makes sites listen.
story.for_makers: In California, Colorado, Connecticut and more, sites must treat it as an opt out. Makers must change ad and data sharing for those visitors. It also tells them who is privacy minded.

use_cases.example: An ad network sees the signal and stops sharing the visitor's data with partners for targeted ads.
A news site hides its 'do not sell my info' link as the setting has already done that job.
A store turns off third party ad pixels for visitors who send the signal.
A game portal limits data sharing with ad partners when it receives the signal from a player in a covered state.
A consent tool stores the opt out and logs that it was honored, for legal proof.
Fingerprinters may use the signal as a clue, so turning it on can make the browser rarer.

risks: Few sites honor it outside the law

technical_bounds: Header only, no proof user understood it
